summary: Helps implementors of IMAP4 make their software work with older IMAP2bis servers and clients. It is meant to be read alongside the earlier specification and the IMAP4 spec. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This is a translation guide so new mail programs can talk to older ones.

questions: how to detect an old imap server
subtitle: How to make an IMAP4 program get along with the older, widely used IMAP2bis servers and clients.

tldr.problem: IMAP2bis was very common and widely distributed with the Pine mailer, but no definitive document describes it, so IMAP4 implementors lack guidance for talking to it.
tldr.mechanism: The memo gives a quick way to detect an old server with the CAPABILITY command and lists, feature by feature, what to use instead of IMAP4 facilities that IMAP2bis lacks.
tldr.outcome: Nothing in it is required by the IMAP4 specification, and implementors decide for themselves whether to support old software.

today: RFC 2061 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 1730. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Compatibility Guide
sections.content:
The Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) has been through several revisions and variants in its 10-year history. Many are extinct or rare, including those in RFC 1064, RFC 1176 and RFC 1203. One variant, IMAP2bis, was very common at the time of writing and widely distributed with the Pine mailer, yet no definitive document describes it.

This memo is meant to be read with RFC 1176 and the then-current IMAP4 specification, RFC 2060. Nothing in it is required by IMAP4. It reflects current knowledge and folklore, and is not complete; for other old variants it points to RFC 1732.
sections.eli5: An old kind of mail program is still all over the place and nobody wrote down exactly how it works, so this memo shares what people have learned.

sections.title: IMAP4 Clients Meeting IMAP2bis Servers
sections.content:
To check a server, try the CAPABILITY command. An OK response lists the supported variants; if the client recognizes none, it should treat the server as IMAP2bis. A BAD response indicates an IMAP2bis or older server.

Most IMAP4 facilities exist in IMAP2bis, but there are exceptions. Use LOGIN instead of AUTHENTICATE, FIND ALL.MAILBOXES instead of LIST, the plain BODY item instead of BODYSTRUCTURE, and BODY[section] with a manual clearing of the \Seen flag instead of BODY.PEEK. The UID items and the CLOSE command have no equivalent.

The bulletin-board commands (BBOARD and related) are best not implemented in new software. Two behaviors differ: IMAP2bis sends TRYCREATE as a separate unsolicited OK response, and it is ambiguous about whether COPY preserves flags or internal dates.
sections.eli5: If the old program does not know a new word, use its older word for the same idea, and a few new ideas just cannot be said at all.

sections.title: IMAP4 Servers Meeting IMAP2bis Clients
sections.content:
The only interoperability problem between an IMAP4 server and a well-written IMAP2bis client is the use of a backslash in quoted strings. It is best avoided by using literals instead of quoted strings when a backslash or a double quote is embedded in the string.

The memo says security issues are not discussed in it.
sections.eli5: Going the other way there is just one snag, a tricky punctuation mark, and you can sidestep it by sending the text a different way.

references.text: RFC 1176, the IMAP2 specification the memo is read alongside.
RFC 2060, the most recent IMAP4 specification at the time.
RFC 1732, for interoperating with other old variants.
